  1. Nov 17 · Subscriber Early Access

    Know the Score

    A credit score is essentially a three digit number that here in the US usually ranges from 300-850. It's a metric that lenders can use to predict your ability to pay back a loan. The higher the number, the more likely you are to be approved for lines of credit. In the United States, your credit score decides where you can live, what car you can drive and whether you can get a loan. It’s supposed to be objective—a precise, omniscient accounting of your financial health, but what started as a simple tool for lenders ended up embedding itself in the lives of most Americans, and feeding the same bias it claimed to solve.     100 Objects #24: White House Solar Panels

  3. 16h ago

    Perfectly Leveraged for the Squat

    Jan Todd was considered by many to be the strongest woman in the world back in the 1970s. She set world records, lifted the Dinnie Stones in Scotland, and wrote the first rulebook for women's powerlifting. Then she became a historian, and uncovered a lost generation of strong women who came before her.  For more, check out Bonnie Tsui's book, On Muscle.   4. 4d ago ·  Bonus

    100 Objects #23: Coin From the Ship of Gold

    On August 20th, 1857 a ship set sail from the Port of San Francisco with 600 people and thousands of pounds of gold. That gold was destined for the vaults of New York City banks, but it never made it. Instead, the ship sank to the bottom of the ocean, taking all that gold with it. Executive Producer Annie Brown sits down with Roman Mars to tell the story of the sinking of the SS Central America and the gold that sparked the first global financial panic, helped fuel the Civil War, and—over a century later—ruined one man’s life. A History of the United States in 100 Objects is a production of 99% Invisible and BBC Studios.   5. Nov 3

    Zone Zero

    Across the West, there's a contentious debate playing out over how to adapt homes and neighborhoods to this era of increasingly extreme wildfire risk. In Berkeley, California, it's become a particularly emotional fight because of a very specific architectural history that began all the way back in the 1890s. Emmett Fitzgerald reports on the new rules about what plants you can grow around your house.   6. Oct 30 ·  Bonus

    100 Objects #22: AOL Disc

    In 1998, the recording industry was thriving. But the company pressing more compact discs than anyone else in America wasn't a record label…it was an internet company: America Online. The AOL Disc was a marketing coup—hugely successful. It’s not an overstatement to say that it’s the campaign that introduced America to the internet. Because of how well it worked, for a while the internet was AOL. And then… it felt like AOL just disappeared. So what happened? Alex Goldman (Reply All, Hyperfixed) finds out. A History of the United States in 100 Objects is a production of 99% Invisible and BBC Studios.   7. Oct 27

    Doktoro Esperanto

    Esperanto is what linguists call a “constructed language.” It isn’t attached to a nation or a region, and it didn’t evolve from another language over time. Instead, nearly 150 years ago, someone decided to sit down and design the whole thing from scratch.  That someone was L. L. Zamenhof, also known as Doktoro Esperanto. He created this language with the hope that it would unite the world under one shared tongue. Today, reporter Katie Thornton tells the story of Doktoro Esperanto’s dream, and what we can all still learn from Esperanto right now. For more, check out Katie's story on Esperanto in Harper's Magazine. Subscribe to SiriusXM Podcasts+ to listen to new episodes of 99% Invisible ad-free and a whole week early.   8. Oct 23 ·  Bonus

    100 Objects #21: Window from the House of D

    In 1932, the Women's House of Detention—New York City's first women's prison—opened in the heart of Greenwich Village. It was opened to make "wayward" women quiet, private, and properly feminine. And the building had one unique feature originally meant to be a sort of kindness—a special kind of window that the women inside could open. Roman Mars and historian Hugh Ryan trace how those special windows had an impact that nobody could have predicted—helping to build a mecca of gay America and, ultimately, a movement. Trailers

  • Trailer

    A History of the United States in 100 Objects Trailer

    America’s 250th birthday calls for a history as sprawling and contradictory as the country itself.  A History of the United States in 100 Objects — hosted by Roman Mars and produced by BBC Studios and 99% Invisible — tells that history one thing at a time. A gold coin from an 1857 shipwreck that triggered a financial panic. An antebellum schoolbook that became an instrument of Black liberation. A ceramic dalmatian from the set of Wheel of Fortune. Or a tiny screw that shows how the US created a hidden industrial empire. Each week, an object opens the door into an extraordinary, often shocking story — about who we’ve been, what we’ve built, and what we’ve allowed ourselves to forget. Some of these objects are well-known. Many are not. But all of them carry the story of how we got to this moment. This is not one narrative. It’s a hundred of them — forming a kaleidoscope that reveals a country stranger and more fascinating than any single telling could capture.
